lessons.title: Fiber Goat Breeds: Angora and Cashmere
lessons.body: In Africa, two main goat breeds produce valuable fiber: Angora and Cashmere. Angora goats are raised for mohair, a long, lustrous fiber. They thrive in dry, temperate regions like the Karoo in South Africa, Lesotho, and parts of Kenya. Angoras need good grazing and shelter from rain. Their fiber grows about 2 cm per month, and they are shorn twice a year. A healthy Angora produces 2â4 kg of mohair per year. Cashmere goats, on the other hand, produce cashmere, a soft, fine undercoat. They are found in colder, high-altitude areas like the Himalayas, but in Africa, they can be raised in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and the Ethiopian Highlands. Cashmere is combed out during molting season, yielding 100â300 g per goat per year. Crossbreeds with local goats can adapt better to African conditions. For smallholders, starting with a few Angoras or Cashmeres can supplement income. However, these breeds require more care than meat goats: they need balanced feed, mineral supplements, and protection from predators. In South Africa, Angora studs are registered, and farmers can join the Mohair Growersâ Association for support. In East Africa, cashmere production is still emerging, but trials show promise. Before buying, check for healthy skin, bright eyes, and no signs of disease. Quarantine new animals for 30 days. With proper management, fiber goats can be a profitable enterprise, especially where there is access to shearing services and fiber buyers.

lessons.title: Shearing and Harvesting Fiber
lessons.body: Shearing Angora goats is done twice a year, typically in spring and autumn. Use sharp electric or manual shears. Before shearing, clean the fleece by removing vegetable matter and dust. Restrain the goat on a shearing board or a clean tarp. Start at the belly and work upwards, keeping the fleece in one piece. A skilled shearer can shear a goat in 3â5 minutes. For cashmere, harvesting is different: during molting season (late spring), use a fine-toothed comb to gently comb out the undercoat. Do this every few days, collecting the soft fiber. Do not pull forcefully. In Africa, many farmers use a metal comb with teeth spaced 2â3 mm apart. After harvesting, store fiber in breathable bags, away from moisture and pests. Avoid mixing different grades. For Angora, skirt the fleece: remove dirty, short, or coarse parts. A good mohair fleece weighs 1.5â2.5 kg. For cashmere, a single combing yields 30â50 g, and total annual yield is 100â300 g. Shearing should be done by a trained person to avoid cuts. If you are new, watch videos or attend a training. In South Africa, mobile shearing teams serve small farms. In Kenya, some cooperatives have shared shears. After shearing, keep goats in a warm, dry place for 24 hours to prevent chilling. Proper harvesting ensures high fiber prices.

lessons.title: Fiber Processing and Cleaning
lessons.body: After harvesting, fiber must be cleaned before spinning. Mohair and cashmere contain grease, dirt, and vegetable matter. Start by sorting: remove any stained, matted, or coarse fibers. Then wash the fiber in warm water (about 50Â°C) with a mild detergent. Do not use hot water or harsh chemicals, as this can damage the fiber. Use a ratio of 10 liters of water to 100 g of detergent for 1 kg of fiber. Soak for 15â20 minutes, then rinse in clean water of the same temperature. Repeat if needed. Squeeze gentlyâdo not wring or twist. Dry in the shade on a clean net or rack. For cashmere, dehairing is crucial to separate the fine undercoat from the coarse guard hair. This can be done by hand or with a dehairing machine. In Africa, small-scale processors use hand cards or drum carders to open and align fibers. Carding removes remaining debris and makes a fluffy batt. For mohair, you may also need to comb it to align the long fibers. After processing, store fiber in a dry, dark place. Clean fiber sells for higher prices. In Lesotho, some cooperatives process mohair locally, adding value. If you plan to sell, keep records of weight before and after cleaning: typically, 1 kg of raw mohair yields 700â800 g of clean fiber. For cashmere, 1 kg of raw yields only 200â300 g of clean down. Proper processing is labor-intensive but increases income.

lessons.title: Spinning and Weaving Basics
lessons.body: Spinning turns fiber into yarn. For beginners, a drop spindle is cheap and portable. You can make one from a wooden dowel and a CD. To spin, draft a small amount of fiber, twist it, and wind onto the spindle. For mohair, a worsted spin gives a smooth, lustrous yarn; for cashmere, a woolen spin gives a soft, fluffy yarn. In Africa, many women spin in groups, sharing techniques. A spinning wheel speeds up production but costs more. You can also use a supported spindle for fine cashmere. After spinning, ply two or more strands together for strength. Weaving is done on a loom. A simple frame loom can be made from wood. You can weave scarves, shawls, or blankets. For mohair, a plain weave shows the fiberâs sheen. For cashmere, a twill weave gives drape. In South Africa, the Karoo weavers use mohair to make luxury textiles. In Kenya, some groups weave cashmere blends. Dyeing can be done with natural dyes from plants like indigo or onion skins. Use alum as a mordant. Always test dye on a small sample. Selling finished products like scarves yields much more than selling raw fiber. A handspun, handwoven mohair scarf can sell for $30â$50 in tourist markets. Start small, practice daily, and join a cooperative for marketing. Remember, quality yarn comes from clean, well-carded fiber.

lessons.title: Grading and Selling Fiber
lessons.body: Grading is sorting fiber by quality to get the best price. For mohair, grade by fiber diameter (micron), length, and cleanliness. The best mohair is fine (under 30 microns), long (over 10 cm), and free of debris. In South Africa, the Mohair Growersâ Association provides official grades: Kid, Young Goat, Adult, and Fine. For cashmere, grade by color (white is most valuable), length (over 3 cm), and fineness (under 19 microns). Use a micrometer to measure diameter, or send samples to a lab. In Africa, many buyers at local markets do not grade, but you can get better prices by selling to cooperatives or export agents. Weigh your fiber accurately and pack in clean, labeled bags. Store in a dry place. Selling options: local markets, fiber cooperatives, online platforms (e.g., Etsy), or direct to spinners. Prices vary: in 2023, South African mohair averaged $25â$35 per kg for adult, $50â$70 for kid. Cashmere can fetch $80â$150 per kg for clean down. To get top prices, build a reputation for consistent quality. Join a cooperative to access better markets. In Lesotho, the Lesotho Mohair Company buys from smallholders. In Kenya, the Kenya Cashmere Initiative links farmers to buyers. Always get a receipt and keep records. Consider adding value by spinning or weaving before selling. A finished product can earn 5â10 times more than raw fiber.

lessons.title: Managing Fiber Goats for Quality
lessons.body: Quality fiber starts with healthy goats. Feed a balanced diet: good pasture, hay, and a supplement of 16% protein pellets. Provide loose minerals, especially sulfur, zinc, and copper, which improve fiber strength. Angora goats need more protein than meat goats. Rotate pastures to prevent parasites. Keep goats in clean, dry sheltersâwet fleeces can mold. Shear or comb regularly to prevent matting. For Angora, shear every 6 months; for cashmere, comb during molting. Keep records of each goatâs fiber yield and quality. Select breeding stock with fine, long fiber. In South Africa, Angora rams are tested for fiber diameter. In Kenya, cashmere goats are selected for down yield. Avoid inbreeding; bring in new genetics every few years. Health care: vaccinate against enterotoxemia and tetanus. Deworm strategically, not routinely. Check for external parasites like lice and mites, which damage fiber. Treat with pour-on insecticides. Provide clean water. Stress reduces fiber quality, so handle goats gently. In hot climates, provide shade. In cold, provide bedding. Keep goats away from thorny bushes that can contaminate fleece. Record everything: birth dates, shearing dates, weights, and fiber grades. Join a breed society for advice. With good management, a small herd of 20 Angoras can produce 60 kg of mohair per year, earning $1,500â$2,000. Cashmere goats yield less but higher value per gram. Consistent quality builds buyer trust.

quiz.q: Which goat breed is primarily raised for mohair?
quiz.explanation: Angora goats are the main source of mohair fiber.

quiz.q: How often are Angora goats typically shorn?
quiz.explanation: Angora goats are shorn twice a year, in spring and autumn.

quiz.q: What is the average annual mohair yield per Angora goat?
quiz.explanation: A healthy Angora produces 2â4 kg of mohair per year.

quiz.q: Cashmere is harvested by:
quiz.explanation: Cashmere is combed out during molting season.

quiz.q: Which region in Africa is known for Angora goat farming?
quiz.explanation: The Karoo in South Africa is a major Angora farming region.

quiz.q: What is the typical yield of cashmere per goat per year?
quiz.explanation: Cashmere goats yield 100â300 g of down per year.

quiz.q: Before shearing, you should:
quiz.explanation: Cleaning the fleece of debris before shearing improves fiber quality.

quiz.q: What tool is used to harvest cashmere?
quiz.explanation: A fine-toothed comb is used to gently comb out cashmere undercoat.

quiz.q: After shearing, goats should be kept:
options: A) In a warm, dry place
B) In a cold, wet place
quiz.explanation: Sheared goats need warmth to prevent chilling.

quiz.q: What is the first step in fiber processing?
quiz.explanation: Sorting removes stained, matted, or coarse fibers before washing.

quiz.q: What water temperature is recommended for washing fiber?
quiz.explanation: Warm water around 50Â°C is effective without damaging fiber.

quiz.q: What is dehairing?
options: A) Removing guard hair from cashmere
quiz.explanation: Dehairing separates the fine undercoat from coarse guard hair in cashmere.

quiz.q: How much clean fiber is obtained from 1 kg of raw mohair?
quiz.explanation: Raw mohair yields about 700â800 g of clean fiber after processing.

quiz.q: Which spinning tool is cheap and portable for beginners?
quiz.explanation: A drop spindle is inexpensive and easy to use for beginners.

quiz.q: What is a common natural mordant used in dyeing?
quiz.explanation: Alum is a common mordant that helps dye bind to fiber.

quiz.q: Which weave is recommended for mohair to show its sheen?
quiz.explanation: Plain weave highlights the natural luster of mohair.

quiz.q: What is the most valuable color of cashmere?
quiz.explanation: White cashmere is most valuable because it can be dyed any color.

quiz.q: Which measurement is used to grade fiber fineness?
quiz.explanation: Fiber diameter is measured in microns; finer fibers are more valuable.

quiz.q: What is the average price range for adult mohair per kg?
quiz.explanation: In 2023, adult mohair averaged $25â$35 per kg.

quiz.q: Which organization supports mohair farmers in South Africa?
quiz.explanation: The Mohair Growersâ Association provides grading and market support.

quiz.q: What supplement improves fiber strength?
quiz.explanation: Sulfur, along with zinc and copper, improves fiber strength.

quiz.q: How often should Angora goats be shorn for quality fiber?
quiz.explanation: Regular shearing every 6 months prevents matting and maintains quality.

quiz.q: What is a common health problem affecting fiber quality?
quiz.explanation: Lice and mites damage fiber and reduce its value.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in fiber goat management?
options: A) To track fiber yield and quality
quiz.explanation: Records help select best breeders and monitor productivity.

quiz.q: What is the typical annual income from 20 Angora goats?
quiz.explanation: 20 Angoras produce about 60 kg mohair, worth $1,500â$2,000.

quiz.q: Which factor does NOT affect fiber quality?
quiz.explanation: Goat color does not affect fiber quality; diet, shelter, and health do.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of carding?
quiz.explanation: Carding opens and aligns fibers for spinning.

quiz.q: Which market channel often gives the best price for fiber?
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives often access better markets and provide grading.

quiz.q: What is a key step to prevent fleece contamination?
quiz.explanation: Thorny bushes can contaminate fleece with vegetable matter.

quiz.q: What is the first step in managing fiber goats for quality?
quiz.explanation: A balanced diet is fundamental for healthy fiber growth.
